title: The Slowest Magic Trick in the Pond

topics.value_lesson: Nothing is wasted — even the tail has a job, feeding the frog it helped to build

spine: We travel station by station along the tadpole's road from jelly egg to first hop, measuring the journey by a tail that shrinks like a pencil being eaten from the eraser end.

segments.text:
We are standing at the warm, shallow edge of Grandfather Shell's pond, just us and the mist, when the old snail slides out from under his lily pad. "Come and see," he says. "Quickly, before the sun drinks the mist."

He points one long eye-stalk at a wobbling blob of jelly eggs. Inside, little black dots are uncurling, one by one, like commas waking up.

"That," says Grandfather Shell, "is where the whole road starts. Jelly to hop, all along this one pond edge. But you have to walk it slowly. One square of the pond-calendar at a time."

Something pops up beside us. Bloop.

A froglet — all legs and stubby tail, half finished and twice as bouncy. "Did somebody say expedition?" he says. "I'm Pippin. Legs: done. Tail: still loading. I am the greatest guide in the pond, and I have been waiting for recruits all morning."

He pats his little tail with one foot. "Don't mind this. It's not falling off. It's my lunch for later."

We look at the tiny black commas. We look at Pippin. How does something that small ever hop?

"One station at a time," says Pippin. "Follow me."

Nix is waiting by the weed, quick as a blink. "Down here," she says. "Quietly now."

We slip below the surface, and the pond turns green and cool and full of little lives. Tadpoles hang in the weed like commas that never woke all the way up. Beside each small head, two feathery tufts wave and wave.

"Gills," whispers Nix. "Like a fish. They fan the water and breathe it. Watch."

We watch. The tufts flutter, flutter, flutter, and every wriggler hangs there drinking the pond through them.

"I hide in this weed too," Nix says, showing us a curled leaf, a hollow stem. "Because I'm mid-journey as well. One day I trade all this water for sky." She says it like a secret she's proud of.

"Will the gills go?" we ask.

"They go," says Nix, and her eyes shine. "The station closes early on this road. What replaces them?" She only smiles. "Next square. You'll see."

We come up dripping, with the green light still in our eyes, and Grandfather Shell chalks one more square on the pond-calendar: gills, seen, just in time.

Pippin leads us along the warm stones, where the sun has made the shallow water bathwater-warm. "This," he says, "is my favourite station. The leg queue."

All along the stones, tadpoles are sprouting legs. Back legs first. Always back legs first. Then front. Nothing jumps the queue.

One tadpole pushes past us with two new back legs dangling, tail still doing all the work. It goes along like a boat with an engine and no oars, wobbling, determined, and we have to press our lips together not to laugh with delight.

"I remember that bit," says Pippin softly. "You have the legs, but nobody's told them what to do yet."

He plants himself on a stone. "Watch the order. Back legs." He waggles them. "Front legs." He waves one at us. "In the right order, every time. The pond doesn't rush." He wobbles, proud as anything, and nearly tips off the stone.

Grandfather Shell slides up beside us, slow as a cloud, and chalks two new squares on the pond-calendar. "Legs," he says. "Twice."

But the legged tadpoles still trail long tails, and not one of them can hop. Pippin taps his own stubby tail and grins. "Something has to happen first," he says. "Guess what's on the menu."

We scramble up the lily pad, and Grandfather Shell is waiting, slow and smiling. "Well?" he says. "What did you find?" We tell him, and he nods like he already knew.

"Now for the heart of the trick," he says. "Gather close." He taps Pippin's stubby tail with one eye-stalk. "This never falls off. Never. It melts back into the body — absorbed, like soup soaking into bread. A packed lunch a tadpole carries behind it. That is why a changing tadpole hardly eats. It is busy digesting its own tail."

We stare. Pippin pats his little tail with one foot, gently this time. "Thank you for the ride," he says to it. "You were delicious." Then he puffs out his chest — and keeps it puffed. "Feel that? Lungs. Two of them. Still loading, but nearly there. One more square and I breathe actual air."

Grandfather Shell sighs a happy snail sigh. "I have a cousin in Mexico," he says, "an axolotl, who keeps her feathery gills forever and never finishes the trick. That is one way to be." He looks at Pippin. "This is another."

Bloop. Pippin bounces. "Last square, recruits. Where should we watch it from?"

"Down here!" Pippin shouts, leading us along the muddy rim where the water laps at our toes. He plants his feet at the very edge, tail stub quivering, and turns to face us with an expression of utmost seriousness. "Witness positions, please. This is it." He opens his mouth wide, wider, widest — and gulps. His throat bobs. His sides swell like two balloons filling for the first time ever. Air. Actual air. "It tastes like outside!" he wheezes, delighted. Then he gathers himself: legs bent, lungs full, tail nearly gone, everything the whole journey was building. He springs. A wobbly, splashy arc through the air — and lands smack on a lily pad, arms windmilling, one foot dangling. "I meant to do that!" We cheer so loudly a dragonfly rattles off its reed. Grandfather Shell slides up beside us, and we pull out our smooth pond pebble. One chalk notch for every square, every stage, every small change — and now the last one, for the hop. Pippin hops down into our cupped hands, damp and warm and thrumming. "Same tadpole," he says softly, looking back at the jelly eggs glistening in the shallows. "Different page." We carry the pebble home in a pocket, heavy as a whole pond, light as a first breath.

"Up! Up!" Pippin cries, and we scramble onto Grandfather Shell's broad lily pad, which dips under our weight like a green trampoline. The old snail settles beside us, eye-stalks pointed down at the water. "Best view in the pond," he says. "I've watched a thousand first hops from this front step." Below us, Pippin takes position. We hold our breath. He opens his mouth — gulps — his throat bobs, his sides swell, air going in for the very first time. Then he launches. Up, up, legs kicking, lungs full, tail a memory — and he lands right beside us on the pad, which boings like a drum. The whole pond seems to wobble with applause. "Told you I'd make it," Pippin pants, grinning. Grandfather Shell reaches into his shell and pulls out the pond-calendar — squares of jelly, nubs of leg, shrinking tails — and turns to the last page. Blank. "For next spring's eggs," he says. "The road is a circle, not a line." We notch our pebble one final time — one mark for every stage we visited — and tuck it safe away. Grandfather Shell raises one slow eye-stalk in a slower wave. Pippin waves back with a foot. "Same time next year, recruits," he says. "I'll be the one with no tail at all."

gathered_but_unused: A tadpole's tail never drops off — it is slowly absorbed back into the body and used as food while the legs grow.
Tadpoles breathe underwater with gills, like fish do, before they grow lungs.
A frog in the middle of changing, with both a tail and legs, is called a froglet.
Frog eggs are laid in a clear jelly that keeps them moist and a little bit safer from hungry mouths.
Back legs grow first, then front legs — always in that order.
While the tail shrinks, the tadpole hardly eats — the tail is its packed lunch.
